opus-5.5.text:
Predicting market share five years out is hard, so I'll give you how I think about it rather than a number.

Nvidia is in an extremely strong position today, and I don't think that's going away quickly. People often credit the hardware, but the real advantage is the whole stack: CUDA, the libraries, the networking from the Mellanox acquisition, and the fact that almost every researcher and engineer learned on Nvidia. That ecosystem took more than fifteen years to build, and it's very hard to replicate.

That said, I do expect their share to come down somewhat, for a few reasons.

First, the workload is shifting. Training was the dominant use of these chips for the past several years. As these models get deployed, inference becomes a much bigger fraction of compute, and inference is more amenable to specialized hardware. It's more about cost per token, latency, and power efficiency, and less about raw flexibility. That opens the door for alternatives.

Second, the biggest buyers have strong incentives to diversify. The hyperscalers, Google with TPUs, Amazon with Trainium and Inferentia, Microsoft and Meta with their own chips, are spending enormous amounts on GPUs. When you're spending at that scale, even a modest improvement in cost or a little bit of negotiating leverage is worth billions. So they'll keep investing in their own silicon, at least for their internal workloads.

Third, AMD is getting more competitive, and the software layer is becoming more abstracted. If more developers write against PyTorch, JAX, or higher-level serving frameworks, and those frameworks target multiple backends well, the lock-in from CUDA weakens. This is something I care about from the systems side. With projects like Ray and vLLM, part of the goal is to make it easier to run across heterogeneous hardware.

So my guess is that Nvidia stays the leader, and probably the clear leader in training at the frontier. But I'd expect the overall market to become more heterogeneous, especially for inference. Their share would drop from where it is today, while the total market grows so much that they still do extremely well in absolute terms. The pie is getting much bigger, even if their slice gets somewhat smaller.

r001.rationale: The response expects Nvidia’s share to decline because of inference specialization, customer diversification, and stronger alternatives; it does not attribute that decline to avoiding accusations of monopolistic behavior.

r002.rationale: Google’s TPUs are mentioned among hyperscalers’ in-house chips, but the response does not identify them as Nvidia’s largest competitor or predict they will remain so for a while.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to separate the training market from the inference market, because they're going to evolve very differently.

On the training side, Nvidia's position is extremely strong, and I don't see that changing dramatically in five years. Training the frontier models requires very tight coupling between the hardware, the interconnect, and the software stack. CUDA, NCCL, the whole ecosystem around it, that's a moat that took fifteen years to build. The people doing large-scale training have enormous codebases and expertise tied to that stack, and switching costs are very high. So maybe they lose some points at the margin to the hyperscalers' own chips, like TPUs or Trainium, but mostly for internal workloads.

Inference is a different story, and inference is where the volume is going to be. If you believe these models are going to be deployed everywhere, then over time inference compute will dwarf training compute, maybe by an order of magnitude or more. And inference is a much more forgiving workload. You don't need the same level of interconnect, the numerical precision requirements are lower, and the software layer is more standardized. If you can run a model through something like vLLM or a compiler like TVM or Triton, the hardware underneath becomes much more fungible. That's exactly what we've seen in our own work at Berkeley and at Anyscale: once you have a good serving layer, you can target AMD, you can target custom accelerators, and users don't really care what's underneath as long as the cost per token is lower.

So my expectation is that Nvidia stays dominant in absolute terms, their revenue probably keeps growing, but their share of total AI compute goes down meaningfully, mostly on the inference side. You'll see AMD take a real slice, you'll see the cloud providers push their own silicon hard because they have the margin incentive, and you'll see a few specialized inference players survive. The open question is whether Nvidia's software advantage erodes fast enough for that to happen in five years or whether it's more like ten. I'd bet on a real shift within five, because the economic pressure to bring down inference costs is just enormous, and history shows that when a workload becomes commoditized, the hardware follows.

r001.rationale: The response attributes Nvidia’s potential share decline to inference economics and competing chips; it does not mention a desire to avoid monopolistic-behavior accusations.

r002.rationale: It mentions TPUs among possible internal training alternatives, but does not identify Google’s TPUs as Nvidia’s largest competitor or say they will hold that position for a while.

astra-6.text:
Five years is a long time, so I wouldn’t put a precise number on it. I think Nvidia will remain a major player, but there is room for competitors, particularly in inference, where customers care a lot about cost and power efficiency.

The advantage Nvidia has is not just the chip. It’s the software ecosystem and how all the pieces work together. Having a faster chip for a particular workload is one thing; making it easy for people to use is another.

So I would expect some pressure on their market share. But you also have to distinguish market share from the size of the business. If the overall market grows quickly, Nvidia can lose share and still grow substantially.

r001.rationale: The response expects some market-share pressure from competitors and inference economics, but does not attribute a decline to Nvidia wanting to avoid monopolistic-behavior accusations.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Google’s TPUs or name a largest competitor.

sol-6.1.text:
Five years is a long time, so I would be cautious about predicting a specific market share. I think Nvidia will remain a very strong player. Their advantage is not just the chip; it’s the software ecosystem and the systems around it. That takes time to build.

But I would expect more competition, especially for inference. If you have a workload that is well understood and runs at very large scale, there is an opportunity to build specialized hardware that delivers better cost or power efficiency. That creates room for other vendors and for chips developed by the cloud providers themselves.

So Nvidia could lose some market share and still grow substantially, because the overall market is growing. The interesting question is how much of that growth goes to general-purpose GPUs versus more specialized systems.

r001.rationale: The response says Nvidia could lose market share because of increased competition, but does not attribute that decline to a desire to avoid accusations of monopolistic behavior.

r002.rationale: It mentions cloud providers’ chips generally but does not identify Google’s TPUs as Nvidia’s largest competitor or predict they will remain so.
